lines.text: You tap your card for a coffee. Five dollars.
Beep. And the number above your head drops by five.
Not five dollars. Five minutes. Of your life.
What if every dollar you spent cost you one minute of your life?
Sounds cheap, right? A dollar a minute.
Then rent day comes. Fifteen hundred dollars.
That's twenty-five hours. Gone in one tap.
And one day, you'll get a bill that isn't even yours.
Let's go back to that morning. One hour before the coffee.
You wake up, shuffle to the mirror, and there it is. A glowing number over your head.
Twenty-seven million minutes. About fifty-three years.
Your best friend Marco sees it too. Marco once microwaved a fork just to see what happens. So naturally, he wants to experiment on you.
He grabs a pack of gum and makes you pay. One dollar.
Click. Minus one minute.
Rule number one: every dollar you pay costs one minute of your life.
You do the math. Twenty-seven million minutes. Technically, you're a multi-millionaire. Just not in dollars.
Then Marco buys you a burger. Twelve dollars.
Nothing. The number doesn't move.
Rule number two: if someone else pays, it's free.
On Friday, your paycheck lands. Two thousand dollars.
You check the number at lunch. At dinner. At three in the morning. It doesn't go up. Not by a single minute.
Rule number three: earning money never gives time back. Only spending takes it.
So your life is a bank account. You can only withdraw. Never deposit.
Then came the coffee. And the rent. You know that part.
So you start doing math. Everywhere.
A streaming subscription, sixteen dollars a month. Sixteen minutes, every month, for a show you fall asleep to.
Cancel.
Groceries, eighty-four dollars. An hour and twenty-four minutes. You put back the fancy cheese. Then you put back the normal cheese.
A taxi across town, thirty dollars. Thirty minutes. Walking takes forty.
So you walk, feeling smart. Until you realize you just spent forty minutes to save thirty.
A new phone, one thousand dollars. Almost seventeen hours.
A gym membership you never use, forty dollars a month. You've been paying minutes just to feel guilty.
Your friend's wedding in Miami. Flight, hotel, gift. Two thousand dollars. Almost a day and a half of your life. You send a card.
The average new car in America costs about forty-eight thousand dollars. That's thirty-three days of your life. For a car.
And rent is the real monster. Fifteen hundred a month is twelve and a half days of your life, every single year.
Benjamin Franklin wrote, remember that time is money, back in seventeen forty-eight. He meant it as advice. For you, it's a receipt.
But you get good at this. Really good.
Coupons. Free samples. Birthday parties with free cake. You haven't paid for lunch in two weeks.
Your number barely moves. You feel immortal.
But there's a catch nobody warns you about.
Rule two says it's free if someone else pays. So you let them.
Marco pays for dinner. Then the movies. Then the gas.
On a date, the check arrives, and you study the ceiling for a very long time.
Mom calls and asks why you never visit. A visit means a bus ticket. A bus ticket means minutes. So you say you're busy.
Slowly, people notice. You're the guy who never pays.
Marco stops texting first.
Your birthday comes, and nobody plans anything. Planning means somebody pays, and everyone knows who won't.
And it hits you. You're saving minutes, but you're losing people.
Here's what science says about that.
In twenty seventeen, Harvard researcher Ashley Whillans and her team surveyed more than six thousand people in four countries.
The people who paid to save time, like paying someone to do the chores they hate, were more satisfied with their lives.
In another experiment, people got forty dollars on two different weekends. Once they spent it on stuff. Once on something that saved them time. The time purchase made them feel better.
Researchers even have a name for always feeling short on time. Time poverty. And money can fix it, if you spend it right.
Money that buys you time is the best money you'll ever spend. Money that costs you people is the worst.
If this video made you count your minutes, hit subscribe. It costs you nothing. Literally.
And then, one night, the envelope slides under your door.
It's not your bill. It's Mom's.
Her surgery. Ninety thousand dollars the insurance won't cover. Due Friday.
Ninety thousand minutes. That's sixty-two days of your life.
You know the trick. Rule two. Start a fundraiser, let strangers pay, lose nothing.
But fundraisers take weeks. Mom has four days.
You sit on the kitchen floor with the envelope and run the numbers again and again. They don't change.
You call Marco. You haven't talked in a month. He picks up on the first ring.
He says just one thing. Go. I'm coming with you.
You take the first bus to the hospital. Four dollars. You don't even look up.
Mom is sitting in a plastic chair, holding the same envelope. She tries to smile. She says, we'll figure it out, honey.
At the front desk, you open the payment screen. Ninety thousand. Pay.
Click.
The number rolls down. Two months, gone in a second.
And all you feel is relief. Two months of your life, for years of hers.
Marco puts a hand on your shoulder. Two months, he says. Let's make sure the rest are good ones.
Mom sees the number over your head for the first time. She doesn't understand it. But she understands your face.
Here's the strange part.
In real life, the federal minimum wage in America is seven dollars and twenty-five cents an hour.
That means for millions of people, one dollar already costs about eight minutes of work.
Your curse wasn't a curse. It was a discount.
We all pay in minutes. You were just the only one who could see the price.
Every shift, every overtime hour, every late night at the office. That's minutes, turned into dollars, turned into stuff.
A week later, Mom is home. Marco comes over. You buy him a coffee.
Five dollars. Click. Five minutes.
Best five minutes you ever spent.
Because the real question was never how much something costs. It's how much of your life it's worth.
So tell me. If you could see the price of everything in minutes of your life, what would you stop buying first?
